edition.window: Orders and decisions passed or reported between 10:00 AM IST on 8 October 2026 and 11:00 AM IST on 9 October 2026

items.caseName: Debashis Nanda v. Gokul Anil Kumar & SCC
items.coram: Justice Mohammad Faiz Alam Khan (Judicial Member) and Naresh Salecha (Technical Member)
items.headline: Going-concern sale starts with liquidation order, not auction notice
items.text: The liquidator of Chamber Constructions was barred by an NCLAT restraint from issuing an auction notice. After the 2025 amendment removed going-concern sales, the NCLT refused to extend his time. The NCLAT held that when the liquidation order directs a going-concern sale, the sale process starts with that order, so the auction notice is only a later step. It set aside the NCLT order and said the liquidator could not be blamed for obeying the restraint.

items.caseName: Manju Sirohi v. Assets Care & Reconstruction Enterprise Ltd & Anup Kumar
items.coram: Justice Mohd Faiz Alam Khan (Judicial Member) and Naresh Salecha (Technical Member)
items.headline: Bankrupt guarantor must repay funds withdrawn after estate vested
items.text: A personal guarantor of Saha Infratech was declared bankrupt and then withdrew about Rs 19 lakh from her bank account. The NCLAT upheld the order directing her to repay it. It held that the estate vests in the bankruptcy trustee from the commencement date, so her later withdrawals dealt with property that was no longer hers. It also held that the jewellery sale proceeds were not excluded assets.

items.caseName: Sonal Sumit Mehta v. Chirag R Shah
items.coram: Justice Yogesh Khanna (Officiating Chairperson); Barun Mitra and Ajai Das Mehrotra (Technical Members)
items.headline: Extending a resolution plan's timeline is not a modification of the plan
items.text: The NCLAT dismissed an application to recall its earlier order, which had extended the time to implement the approved resolution plan for Krystal Stone Exports. The delay in handing over the debtor's Jaipur property, part of which a third party occupied, was not the resolution applicant's fault. The tribunal said that extending payment timelines does not modify an approved plan.

items.caseName: Darshan Singh Anand v. Bimla Devi Jindal & Ors
items.coram: Kaushalendra Kumar Singh (Technical Member) and Khetrabasi Biswal (Judicial Member)
items.headline: Being a director alone does not create fraudulent trading liability
items.text: The resolution professional of Vikas WSP sought Section 66 action against 18 former directors, relying on a draft transaction audit report. The final audit report found no fraud. The NCLT held that liability needs proof that a person personally took part with dishonest intent, and that holding a directorship or committee seat is not enough. It dismissed the application.

items.caseName: Asier Metal Private Limited v. Polycab India Limited
items.coram: Shammi Khan (Judicial Member) and Sanjeev Sharma (Technical Member)
items.headline: Polycab admitted to CIRP over Rs 2.78 cr unpaid ingot supplies
items.text: An aluminium ingot supplier claimed Rs 2.78 crore in unpaid invoices from Polycab. Polycab argued that the bills were provisional and raised a large counterclaim. The NCLT found that the goods had been received and that the disputes surfaced only after the demand notice, without contemporaneous records. It admitted the Section 9 petition and appointed an interim resolution professional.

items.caseName: Sujatha Venkateswaran v. Registrar of Companies, Chennai
items.coram: Sanjiv Jain (Judicial Member) and Venkataraman Subramaniam (Technical Member)
items.headline: Struck-off company can still be wound up to realise its assets
items.text: A shareholder sought the winding up of Jaipriya Holdings, which was struck off in 2011 but still held listed shares and owed loans to shareholders. The NCLT held that Section 248(8) keeps its power to wind up a struck-off company. It found winding up just and equitable, admitted the petition and appointed a provisional liquidator.

items.caseName: Omkara Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. v. ESPO Developers Pvt. Ltd.
items.coram: Ashok Kumar Bhardwaj (Judicial Member) and Atul Chaturvedi (Technical Member)
items.headline: Part payment under failed settlement no bar to Rs 164 cr CIRP
items.text: The NCLT admitted Omkara ARC's Section 7 petition against ESPO Developers. It held that the Rs 77.03 crore paid under a settlement did not discharge the debt, because the settlement's benefits depended on meeting all its terms. A pending arbitration did not stop the tribunal from deciding the petition, and the allegation of malicious filing was rejected.

items.caseName: State Bank of India v. Bhakti Extractions Private Limited
items.coram: Sameer Kakar (Technical Member) and Nilesh Sharma (Judicial Member)
items.headline: MSME revival framework can't block SBI plea above Rs 25 cr exposure
items.text: The NCLT admitted SBI's Section 7 petition over a Rs 66.27 crore default. The debtor relied on the RBI MSME revival framework, but the tribunal noted that the framework covers only loan exposure up to Rs 25 crore and that no restructuring application had been made. Once default is shown, the debtor's ability to pay need not be examined.

items.caseName: Insta Capital Pvt Ltd & Richbond Capital Pvt Ltd v. Shubh Food Industries Ltd
items.headline: Joint financial creditors may club dues to cross Rs 1 cr threshold
items.text: Two financial creditors filed a joint Section 7 application against Shubh Food Industries, claiming a combined default of about Rs 1.14 crore. The NCLT held that co-applicants can combine their defaults to meet the Rs 1 crore minimum. It found the statutory requirements met and admitted the company into insolvency.

items.headline: Running-account dues with trade discounts fall due at year-end
items.text: In a Section 9 petition over about Rs 1.92 crore, the NCLT held that limitation runs from when the operational debt became payable, not from when the goods were delivered. Because the parties ran an account with post-supply trade discounts, the liability crystallised on 31 March 2023. The petition, filed in March 2026, was therefore within time and CIRP was admitted.

items.caseName: M/s North East Carriers Private Limited v. Commissioner of CGST & CX, Guwahati
items.coram: R. Muralidhar (Judicial Member) and K. Anpazhakan (Technical Member)
items.headline: Transporter not liable for GTA tax already paid by recipients
items.text: The department confirmed a demand of about Rs 1.2 crore against a road transporter, based largely on income tax data. CESTAT held that the freight-paying recipients were liable under reverse charge, so taxing the transporter as well would be double taxation. It also rejected the extended limitation period and set aside the demand, interest and the Section 78 penalty, keeping only a Rs 10,000 penalty.

items.caseName: M/s Agribiotech Industries Ltd. v. Commissioner, CGST & Central Excise, Alwar
items.coram: Ashok Jindal (Judicial Member) and P.V. Subba Rao (Technical Member)
items.headline: Contract bottling of liquor for a brand owner attracts service tax
items.text: Agribiotech made and bottled liquor for Allied Blenders under a revenue-sharing arrangement and argued that this was manufacture, not a service. CESTAT followed the Delhi High Court's Carlsberg India ruling and held the activity to be a taxable service under the negative-list regime. It dismissed the appeals.

items.caseName: Shri R. Dewakar v. Commissioner of Customs (Seaport, Imports)
items.coram: Ajayan T.V. (Judicial Member) and M. Ajit Kumar (Technical Member)
items.headline: Hayabusa split across two ports treated as one bike for duty
items.text: Two consignments of parts from one Singapore supplier landed at Tuticorin and Chennai four days apart. Markings, inspection reports and a foreign number plate showed that they came from a single registered Suzuki Hayabusa. CESTAT upheld the roughly Rs 10.36 lakh duty and confiscation, but because of the long delay it removed joint liability and reduced the penalties and fines.

items.headline: Invoices, bank records and ITRs prove lawful source of seized gold
items.text: Railway police in Guwahati seized gold from the appellant, Kanheya Lal, on a tip that it was smuggled. CESTAT found that his purchase invoices, bank statements and income tax returns discharged the Section 123 burden, and that the revenue failed to rebut them. It ordered the gold to be released.
